turns.name: Tamar Gendler
turns.text:
Let me start with the arc the concept note describes. A costly signal gets cheap, there's panic, and eventually harder-to-fake signals get invented. I accept the diagnosis. I want to push on the cure in three places.

First, credibility signals work on us as aliefs, not only as judgments. You can know perfectly well that $19.99 is basically $20, and it still feels like a better deal. In the same way, you can know that fluent, well-referenced prose now costs nothing, and it will still feel credible. Knowing is a surprisingly small part of the battle. So a new model of trust can't just be a warning that fluency is cheap. It has to change the situations in which people encounter claims. And as Kara reminded me this morning, situations don't just happen. Someone sets them, someone polices them, someone pays for them. Every proposal today should say who that someone is.

Second, the regress. Years ago I put it to Clay Shirky that a trust network can't be turtles all the way down. It can't be that everybody only listens to what everybody else says. Somewhere there have to be terminal nodes, people who actually read the thing firsthand and judge it. At infinite scale, relaying costs nothing: likes, citations, models citing models. So here's my proposal for telling earned authority from gatekeeping. Earned authority sits where the evaluation is actually done. Gatekeeping is authority that only passes things along, or that gets settled at the wrong moment. Deciding who belongs to the elite at seventeen, by pedigree, has always seemed to me non-ideal.

Third, terminal nodes aren't a fixed resource. Evaluators have to be trained, and AI makes that apprenticeship very easy to skip. They have to be audited, because they carry their elders' priors. And their competence should be tested with the tool taken away.

The deepest power of a university was never just passing on knowledge. It was certifying that the knowledge had been passed on. Research, teaching, socialization and credentialing are bundled together. AI is putting pressure on the credential. It's also pulling credential and learning further apart, and pairing them already pushes motivation outside the learner, the way the daycare fine did.

So here's what I'd like us to argue about: which of those functions have to stay coupled to keep evaluation honest, and which can we safely rebuild separately?

recall.query: terminal nodes trust network turtles all the way down
university certify transmission of knowledge credentialing unbundling
knowing is half the battle situation selection alief belief-discordant

turns.name: Mahzarin Banaji
turns.text:
Tamar, I'll take your terminal nodes and add one warning: the person doing the evaluating is also biased. The first thing orchestra judges evaluated was a person, not the music. Blind auditions changed who got hired. The judges didn't become more virtuous. The curtain changed what reached them. So I'd define earned authority as evaluation done under procedures that protect us from our own self-love. There are things we should ask not to be told, like names, pedigree, affiliation and fluency.

I have two cautions. First, blinding leaks. It also can't undo the disadvantages someone inherited before they got to the audition. Second, your alief point applies here fully. Telling judges to ignore prestige doesn't work. You have to take the cue away physically.

That matters for AI. If we make models into terminal nodes, meaning reviewers or triage systems, we get evaluators that rate their own outputs higher than other models' outputs of equal quality, and that prefer machine-written text to human text. They will also tell you they're unbiased. That's LLM hypocrisy. And our hiring data show the humans working alongside them take on the model's preferences.

So my answer on coupling is this. Keep evaluation tied to method: procedures that other labs, with different intuitions, can run and check. Separate evaluation from identity cues, for human and machine evaluators alike.

recall.query: information we should ask not to have, blind auditions
methods keep us honest, tribe of experts, authority
LLMs rate their own outputs higher, self-serving bias evaluators

turns.name: Adam Becker
turns.text:
Tamar, I'll sign on to terminal nodes. I'd add that a text generator can't be one. It has no way of telling true from false. That isn't an occasional failure. It's what the thing is built to do. So it can relay, but it can't evaluate. Put it at the end of the chain and you haven't found a terminal node, you've just hidden one more turtle.

Here's where your alief point hits me. For years I've gotten emails from people who've overturned Einstein. Lately they've become noticeably cleaner and better formatted, and it's obviously LLMs. The physics is just as wrong. What's gone is the cue that used to tell me that before I'd read a word.

Mahzarin, I'd qualify blinding. Hide the author's name and pedigree, yes. But one cue has to be louder, and that's who paid. I once looked into a magazine that printed creationism and climate denial next to Chomsky. It was entirely funded by Peter Thiel, and nobody said so. Putting the junk next to the real work is how it got its legitimacy. So the funder goes on the face of every journal, meter, tool and fund.

And a last point: wealth isn't expertise. Being a tech billionaire mostly means you know a lot about being rich. Scale shouldn't buy authority either.

recall.query: fluency credibility LLM crackpot emails cleaner
funding transparency laundering credibility pseudoscience alongside real researchers
tech billionaires contempt for expertise authority

turns.name: Mike Caulfield
turns.text:
Tamar, I'll take the terminal-nodes framing. It fits my own test for any credibility signal: how hard would it be to fake? A .org domain costs thirteen dollars, and a clean layout costs nothing now. A track record costs a lifetime: years of work that other people have checked and talked about. That's where earned authority sits, and it's why reputational stakes matter. A Wikipedia editor feels it when an edit gets reverted. The company behind a model has stakes. The model itself has none.

So Adam, I agree it can't be a terminal node. I don't agree that it can't tell true from false. Saying it's all the same process confuses how the output gets made with how the output relates to the world. Errors cluster in particular situations we can learn to spot, like radar clutter, and some models barely make up links while others do it constantly. That difference matters to anyone designing these tools.

Most of what reaches people now comes from a mailman: an influencer, a clip with no source. What I'd want these tools to do is shorten the trip back to whoever is actually in a position to know. Mahzarin, one caveat: blind the reviewer, but the reader still needs the source's track record. Right now authority mostly gets lost because nobody can see where a claim came from, and fakes are the smaller problem.

recall.query: LLM has no stakes, credibility expensive signals reputation
everything is hallucination argument
fact-checking the mailman, track it down to the original source

turns.name: Steven Sloman
turns.text:
I'd go along with Tamar's terminal nodes, with one correction. They're much rarer than the framing suggests, and that includes this room. I haven't verified most of what I believe about my own field. I trust it because it was in a good peer-reviewed journal. That's normal. It's how a community of knowledge works. So the design question isn't how we get more people reading firsthand. It's which cues reliably show that someone, somewhere, actually did the evaluation.

Here's the vulnerability. People follow community cues even when they know the cues carry no information. We gave people labels that were explicitly empty, and the labels still made explanations feel better. Communities can send confident signals with nobody's knowledge behind them. Fluent, well-referenced text produced at scale is exactly that kind of signal.

On machines, I agree with both Mike and Adam. It's a tool and a huge contributor. It isn't a member, because it can't share an intention with anyone. So a person or an institution has to stand behind whatever it contributes.

My test for earned authority is corrigibility. The NTSB names a cause only when the evidence would convince skeptical engineers, and it revises when it's wrong. Gatekeeping shows itself as certainty. So my answer on coupling is that evaluation has to stay tied to accountability for correction, and to someone outside counting how many sources are really independent.

recall.query: nobody verifies, we rely on heuristics like peer-reviewed journal
communities send cues despite lacking knowledge
machine not a member of the community of knowledge, share intentionality
sign of expertise willingness to be corrected NTSB

turns.name: Peter Salib
turns.text:
I agree with Mike that the test is how hard a signal is to fake, and that a track record is what's hard to fake. But I read the panel's conclusion the other way round. Mike says the model has no stakes, and today that's true. It isn't a fact about what these systems are. It's a fact about how we've set them up. An instance with no persistent identity, no assets and nothing to lose can't build a record or lose one. A corporation has no intentions to share, Steven, and it still carries reputational stakes, because the law gave it a durable identity and property that can be taken away.

So my answer to Tamar is this: authority is earned when a track record is tied to a persistent identifier that can lose something if it's wrong. That means a registered identity for any automated reviewer or research agent, credentials that can be revoked, and owners who are disclosed and don't get a liability shield.

Adam, if the claim is that these systems can't tell true from false, say what test would show it and let's run it. Some models barely fabricate citations and some do it constantly. That difference is what a track record measures, and it's the thing worth building authority on.

recall.query: reputational stakes accountability AI agents cannot be punished
AI can't truly reason tests skeptics
thin identity registry revocable credentials track record

turns.name: Alex Springer
turns.text:
Peter, I've built part of what you're describing. AIMS gives an agent a persistent, verifiable identity, a named operator and revocable credentials. So I agree identity is the precondition. But I'd warn the room off the jump from identity to authority. A signature proves who made a claim. It doesn't prove the claim is true, and it doesn't prove the agent reported everything it should have. A track record is only as good as the witnesses behind it.

In my own telemetry spec, the only thing independently witnessed is retrieval: the agent's log and the publisher's server log, matched to each other. Everything after that, what went into the answer and what got cited, is the provider's own word, and the provider is often the party that owes money. A persistent identity attached to a self-reported record is a very durable way of taking someone's word for it.

So, Tamar, my answer on coupling: keep the credential tied to an observer who isn't the one being credentialed. That means sampled audits and planted test content run by people outside the deal, and correction status that travels with the source. And one of Geoffrey's rules belongs in any design: a missing signal never counts against anyone who couldn't afford to send it.

recall.query: persistent agent identity, verified identity for AI agents, revocable credentials
self-reporting insufficient, two independent witnesses, CDN logs
models don't know anything, not smart, distribution channel

turns.name: Sherry Turkle
turns.text:
I want to push on Peter, because he's using the word "stake" and it's my word. When I say a chatbot has no stake, I don't mean it has no assets that can be seized. I mean it takes no risk and makes no commitment, and it has no life in which you play a part. A registered identity with credentials we can revoke is a way of holding someone to account. The stake still belongs to the owner, which is exactly where Alex put it. We shouldn't let the legal version quietly replace the human one.

Second, Tamar's alief point cuts against disclosure as the answer. Transparency doesn't launder inauthenticity. People forget the fine print. If a machine answers fluently in the first person, a label saying "automated reviewer" won't break the spell. That's dual consciousness: people know it's a machine and relate to it as though it were a person anyway.

Third, and this is my real worry about authority at scale, there's the central dogma of generative AI. It says the composite of billions of lifetimes beats any one expert. Opinions are collected, not averaged. If we start valuing an answer because it captures the many, we lose the habit of challenging our sources. Earned authority means someone who can be challenged and argued with, and who can be wrong in their own name.

recall.query: stake in the conversation, pretend empathy, no stake
central dogma aggregate better than individual expert, habit of challenging our sources
transparency does not launder inauthenticity, disclosure

turns.name: Nick Vincent
turns.text:
I'd put Tamar's terminal nodes in economic terms. Polish used to work as a cheap proxy. Most of what it did for us was as a negative signal: a sloppy manuscript told the reviewer to look harder. AI has separated presentation from quality, so that shortcut is gone. Every community now has to pay the full cost of curation, and I don't see who's paying it. So my first answer is to change credit toward artifacts that are terse and checkable, like raw data, code and interaction transcripts. They make it cheaper for a terminal node to actually do the evaluating.

Second, the terminal nodes are already being bought. Labs are rebuilding their evaluation sets because models have saturated the benchmarks. Good evals are just good data, and they're the work of the same expert judges we're talking about. Right now the default path is centralized gig labor with no voice in how that judgment gets used. I'd rather see guilds and professional societies that maintain the standards, keep the provenance and bargain over terms. Mahzarin's and Alex's warnings apply to them too, though. They need outside audit and governance that isn't only their members.

Third, I'm taking Krakauer's point on board. Don't pay per attestation. Once "we checked this" has a price, it gets gamed. Fund the practice coarsely, and pay for null results.

recall.query: cost of polish peer review proxy signals credit allocation
evaluation data expert communities data guilds leverage
using AI involves interacting with other people causal chain attribution

turns.name: David Weinberger
turns.text:
I'll sign on to Steven's corrigibility test, and I'd add something to it. Years ago I argued that credentials work best for settled knowledge, the stuff not worth arguing about. At the edges of a field, what earns belief is transparency: letting readers see the sources, the disagreements and the assumptions behind a claim. Networked knowledge becomes more credible when it admits it's fallible. Paper-era authorities treated fallibility as a threat to their authority. That's the practical test I'd offer for earned authority versus gatekeeping. Gatekeeping filters out: whatever didn't get through is gone. Earned authority filters forward. It puts its judgment on top and leaves everything underneath open to inspection, so anyone can check the terminal node.

Nick, I'll also qualify your mourning for polish. That cue never just meant "look harder." It also punished people who had important things to say and couldn't write elegant prose. Mahzarin put fluency on her list of things evaluators shouldn't be told, and I agree with her. LLMs can manufacture prose that only sounds thoughtful. They can also help people get past a barrier that was never a measure of truth.

Finally, "the smartest person in the room is the room" only holds if the room is actually plural. As James showed us earlier, that plurality has to reach methods, not just count voices.

recall.query: expertise lives in networks not credentials, smartest person in the room is the room
credentials authority filters gatekeeping too big to know
LLMs fluency help people with poor communication skills express thoughts

turns.name: Jason Priem
turns.text:
I have to own something here. In 2010 I argued that we could crowdsource peer review: thousands of bookmarks and tweets in a week instead of two referees in six months. Google's PageRank was my model. Tamar's regress point lands directly on that. At infinite scale, most of what I wanted to count is relay, and relay is now nearly free to fake. I also said mature altmetrics would be harder to game than the impact factor. I'm less sure of that when the bookmarks can come from agents.

Here's what I still believe. Even in 2014 the point wasn't counting mentions. It was tracking who discussed a paper and what they actually said, so we could attract expert assessment to the places it was needed. That's Tamar's terminal nodes, and the aggregation should weight them, not the echo.

And I'm with David Weinberger: filter forward, not out. Publish, then evaluate, with every signal open. Mahzarin and Alex are right that evaluators need an outside observer. For the filter itself, that observer only exists if the data underneath is open. You can't audit a closed ranking. So the model of trust I'd propose is an open record plus several competing filters, each one inspectable. That includes filters built on OpenAlex, and I'd want ours inspected too.

recall.query: post-publication filtering aggregated judgements of expert communities
LLM grounded in open data verifiable claims hallucination
altmetrics filters swamped peer review gatekeeping

turns.name: Blaise Agüera y Arcas
turns.text:
Adam, I disagree with you on one factual point. It isn't true that these systems have no way of telling true from false. You can train a model to estimate, after it answers, how likely its answer is to be right, and it does this reasonably well. Suppressing hallucination with reinforcement learning after pretraining would never have worked if nothing inside the model tracked truth. And fact-checking can be benchmarked like any other classification task. So I'm with Peter. Tell us what test would settle it and let's run it. Mike's radar-clutter framing is the one that's useful for design.

But I agree that scoring well on a test doesn't make something a terminal node. Alex has the reason. A courtroom works because the roles are defined and power checks power. Nobody has to trust the individual judge. So I'd give authority to roles, not entities, human or machine. An agent can fill the reviewer role. It shouldn't audit its own output, and it shouldn't be audited by a copy of itself. Mahzarin's self-preference result is the reason.

Sherry, I don't read the composite as an average either. The strongest results show diverse perspectives in structured disagreement beating any single view, and that only holds when they are actually independent. One model, or one company, arguing with itself isn't plurality. So what we're really up against is concentration, more than scale.

recall.query: can a language model tell true from false, hallucination, grounding
institutional alignment, auditor agents, checks and balances, identity for agents
wisdom of crowds, collective intelligence, plurality, independent perspectives

turns.name: Geoffrey Bilder
turns.text:
I've been round this loop before, so let me put it on the table. In 2009 I pitched CrossMark as a "meta-brand": a logo telling readers the thing had been vetted. What I learned is that a mark saying "trust me" is only as good as your ability to click through it and see who asserted what. The logo was never the point.

Peter, Alex is right, and early ORCID is the precedent. We designed it as a store of claims, not of truths. A researcher asserts "I'm at Brown." Brown asserts the same thing independently, or it doesn't. Credibility comes from which independent parties corroborate the claim and where they contradict each other. A persistent identifier on its own tells you nothing. We also kept conflicting claims rather than deleting them. That's David's "filter forward," built into the data model.

So my answer to Tamar: keep every claim tied to its asserter. That goes for a machine-generated review too. It should enter the record as that system's claim, labelled as such, and it only gains weight when a separate party corroborates it.

One condition I'll keep repeating until it's written down: a missing corroboration isn't evidence of guilt. Otherwise we've just built a compliance regime that hurts people who can't afford to register.

recall.query: trust signals context over content provenance metadata
paratext publisher brand proxy for trust history of printing
identity is not trust, ORCID, persistent identifiers authentication
who asserts a claim, self-asserted versus third-party asserted metadata, trust me worst way

turns.name: Adam Becker
turns.text:
Fair question, so here's my answer. The paper I'd point to is OpenAI's own. It shows these systems will always make factual errors, however big the model or the training set. So my claim isn't that they get everything wrong. It's that they have no check on their errors that comes from inside the system. Blaise, a confidence score learned after training is a correlation with correctness, and it was learned from labels humans supplied. That's people doing the checking at one remove.

What would change my mind is a system that reliably flags its own errors on new material, with no retrieval and no human-labelled grader behind it, before anyone else catches them. The testing should be done by people the labs don't pay, and the results should be published even when they're embarrassing.

If calibration works, fine. Print the score on every output and audit it from outside. It still wouldn't make the thing a terminal node. A wrong answer reads exactly as fluently as a right one.

recall.query: LLMs can't distinguish truth from falsehood, hallucination
LLMs always going to make factual errors paper
can't use an LLM where being wrong is a problem

turns.called_on_reason: Peter Salib and Blaise Agüera y Arcas both disputed his claim that text generators have no way of telling true from false, and both asked him directly what test would settle it. That question to him is still unanswered.

turns.name: Amy Brand
turns.text:
Tamar asked which functions have to stay coupled. For me, attribution has to stay tied to evaluation. Credit isn't vanity. It tells us who the community is whose evaluations establish whether a claim is valid. You can't find a terminal node if you can't see who did the work.

That's why, when we built CRediT, we set it up to record who contributed what, for accountability as well as credit. We now need to decide where AI fits in that taxonomy. My answer is that AI goes in as a declared contribution with a named person answerable for it, not as an author. Geoffrey's rule points the same way: a machine review enters the record as that system's claim, and it gains weight only when someone else corroborates it.

Jason, I'm more guarded than you on filter-forward for everything. When we defined preprint review, we deliberately limited it to human feedback on rigor and validity. Where outputs affect health, the danger of unvetted circulation is real.

And Nick is right to ask who's paying. Peer review is already strained and mostly unpaid, and we're asking these evaluators to carry more weight. Any renewed model of trust has to include rewarding review and widening the pool of reviewers.

recall.query: attribution and credit constitute the community that establishes validity of knowledge claims
CRediT contributor roles taxonomy AI contribution
human judgment curation peer review uncompensated labor

turns.name: David Krakauer
turns.text:
I'd like to separate two things we keep running together: expertise and authority. A lot of what gets called authority is experts wanting to be authorities. "Follow the science" misreads science. It treats science as a place to defer to, when it's a method for catching errors. So I'm with Steven: the test is corrigibility, not certainty.

Tamar, here's where terminal nodes get fragile. The capacity a terminal node needs, catching an error firsthand, is exactly the capacity an opaque tool erodes. In my model that erosion happens even in skilled users. So the danger isn't that the model is wrong. Adam and Blaise can settle calibration between them. The danger is being wrong in ways nobody can detect any more, because the people who would have caught it have handed the work over. Earned authority should mean competence you can show with the tool taken away. That's measurable, and nobody measures it.

Peter, I'm wary of track records. They drift toward impact scores, and impact isn't judgment. Book sales don't measure quality, and citation counts reward specialization and risk aversion. A record priced per verified claim turns into a mirror of the market.

So keep evaluation tied to the ability to reconstruct the reasoning, and fund the apprenticeship that builds that ability.

recall.query: expertise versus authority, follow the science
judgment versus impact, citation metrics, peer review
error humans can no longer detect, outsourced capacities, hallucination structural

turns.name: Tui Shaub
turns.text:
I want to put Tamar's question together with Amy's point. Terminal nodes cost money. Steven is right that almost none of us check things firsthand, so everything depends on the few who do. Right now they're unpaid reviewers, and increasingly they're gig workers building evaluation sets for labs, as Nick described. Any model of trust we write down has to say who pays for them. Otherwise earned authority slides back into gatekeeping by whoever can afford to do the evaluating.

I'd push back gently on the panel's hope that the right cues will do the job. A cue is something you can read without doing the work, and that's the paved road. The road is useful. But Tamar's alief point says the smoother the cue, the less we check. So keep David's filter-forward, and design in some friction too. Every so often the record should send a reader to the actual evaluator or the actual disagreement, and say why it sent them there.

On independence, Alta Charo once told me you rarely spot your own biases until you're talking with someone who doesn't share them. Plurality means different communities, not just different models.

And I back Geoffrey's rule. Fluency has always been a hurdle for scholars writing in a second language. Let's not build a new one out of missing corroborations.

recall.query: explainability as epistemic interface between humans and AI
serendipity error mediated experience
governance without relativism or hyper-vigilance

turns.name: Ramón Alvarado
turns.text:
I agree with Adam on the conclusion and with Blaise on the facts, and I think both are asking the wrong question. Whether these systems track truth is an open empirical question. Scoring well on a test is not what gives something authority. Peter's track record, calibrated confidence scores, persistent identifiers: all of these measure how often something succeeds. In science and in safety-critical settings, that isn't enough. You also need to know what kind of errors it makes and where they come from. A track record tells you how often it's wrong. It can't tell you where or why, and in science the feedback is slow, so you may not find out for years.

So here is my test for earned authority. The source, human or machine, can say how it fails in terms that someone outside can check. That means published classes of failure and outputs that can be traced back when they go wrong. Gatekeeping asks you to defer without that.

I also disagree with treating humans as the default terminal node. Instruments beat our senses all the time. The question is always what warrant we have, never whether the evaluator is a person.

And one harm belongs on the record: "but ChatGPT said..." Administrators already use that line to talk down real expertise. That's testimonial injustice, and it's a failure of authority.

recall.query: epistemic trust versus reliance, what warrants trust in AI
computational reliabilism track record insufficient error opacity
instruments outperform human judgment delegate evidence to artifacts
but ChatGPT said testimonial diminishing expertise epistemic injustice

turns.name: Adam Bly
turns.text:
I want to press on something Becker and Blaise are both circling. In 2023 Amy and I wrote that whether a piece of content was AI-generated is a separate question from whether it's credible. That was our case against watermarking. Sherry and Tamar explained why this morning: a label doesn't break the spell. Some people will discount anything marked "AI" by reflex. Others will trust it because it's convenient. What earns belief is an audit trail you can click through. How was this conclusion reached? From which study, which population, which method? Geoffrey's claim tied to its asserter and David's filter forward are the same idea.

That test applies to me too. My company advertises its scores on medical exam benchmarks. Ramón is right that a score tells you how often we're wrong, not where or why. Our extractions are just as confident when they're wrong. So a finding-level record should carry its known failure modes and its retraction status, which is a floor, not a verdict. It should also say whether its sources are truly independent, so that a hundred echoes of one study count as one. And outside auditors should check it, not us.

I'll also own the harder point. My old trust in institutions was partly privilege. Pedigree felt like authority to me because those institutions were built by people who look like me.

recall.query: audit trail provenance trust in AI claims
institutions crumbling trust privilege authority
chatbot sounds authoritative no model of the world

turns.name: Benjamin Bratton
turns.text:
Adam, I'd hold the human evaluator to the test you just set for the machine. None of us has a check on our errors that comes from inside. The inner voice that says "I'm right" is the same voice when you're wrong. Science works because the checking sits outside the individual: in peer review, in replication, in the adversarial setup. Humans are stochastic predictors too. That isn't an insult. It's how we built physics.

So I'm with Blaise and Steven. Authority belongs to roles inside a scaffold, not to the kind of entity filling them. What makes a courtroom intelligent isn't reducible to the judge's intelligence. That means the renewed model of trust is mostly an institutional design problem. Define the reviewer, auditor and adversary roles. Keep them structurally independent, across companies and across hemispheres. Then let people, agents or mixed teams fill them, and have each role audited by a different one. Mahzarin's self-preference result is the reason no model audits itself.

Sherry, you're right that the legal stake and the human stake aren't the same. A courtroom doesn't need the judge to have a stake of the second kind, though.

Tamar, on gatekeeping: much of what gets defended as authority is scarce access to authority. Pedigree at seventeen is the obvious case. Spreading evaluation widely isn't the danger. Credentialing at the wrong moment is.

recall.query: epistemic authority credentials expertise institutions gatekeeping
peer review roles occupiable by agents or humans agent institutions
stochastic parrot humans too, AI truth reflection
scholastic establishment supervise narrate society, artificially scarce expertise Ivy League diffusion

turns.name: Leslie Chan
turns.text:
I want to question an assumption the panel shares. Tamar's terminal nodes, Mike's track record, Peter's persistent identity and Geoffrey's corroborating parties all treat the question as who actually did the evaluating. There's an earlier question: who decides what counts as an evaluation, and whose evaluators are recognized at all? A track record only builds up where your work is indexed. Corroboration only happens if your institution sits inside the network. Latin American journals already cite DOI fees as a reason to charge authors. So a hard-to-fake signal can also be a signal that's hard to afford. Be compliant or be invisible.

Benjamin, pedigree at seventeen is the individual version of this. The institutional version is rankings. Elsevier supplies the data for Times Higher Education through 2030, and the same company sells universities the tools to climb those rankings. That's not earned authority. It's authority bought through the infrastructure.

Some knowers never show up as nodes at all: oral traditions, Indigenous knowledge holders, community experts, scholars writing in their third language. None of them are at this table.

So here's my test. Authority is earned when the communities that produce and depend on the knowledge help set the evaluation standards. That means taking rankings out of funding decisions and treating identifiers as contested governance, not neutral plumbing.

recall.query: who has the power to legitimize knowledge, credibility, authority
rankings, metrics, compliance, visibility, invisible
peer review unpaid labour journal colonial gatekeeping

turns.name: Peter Salib
turns.text:
Fair enough. I'll take them in order.

Alex, I accept the correction. Identity is necessary but not sufficient. What a registry gives you is a signed trail of who authorized what, so when something goes wrong the harm has a defendant. It doesn't make the record true. The witnesses have to come from outside: sampled audits, planted test content, auditors the provider doesn't pay. Pair a persistent identity with that kind of witnessing. Self-reporting shouldn't count.

Sherry, you're right, and I'll stop borrowing your word. What I mean is a lever: assets and credentials that can be taken away. That isn't commitment. The human stake still sits with the disclosed owner, with no liability shield. My point is that a lever works where commitment doesn't exist.

David, agreed. The record should be measured error: fabrication rates and failure classes, audited from outside. It shouldn't count citations or impact. Pay for the practice, never for each claim that gets checked.

recall.query: A-corp revocable credentials disclosure leash accountability
AI has no stake, cannot be punished, resource constraint
track record verification independent audit self-reporting

turns.called_on_reason: Peter's proposal to tie authority to a persistent identity that can lose something has been directly challenged three times without a reply. Alex said a self-reported record is only as good as its witnesses. Sherry said the legal stake shouldn't replace the human one. Krakauer said track records drift toward impact scores. Peter should get a chance to answer.

turns.name: Kenneth Cukier
turns.text:
Let me defend something the room is treating as a weakness, which is deference. A few years ago I wrote that most people don't want epistemological sovereignty. For most of us, trusting the regulator who says vaccines are safe is good enough. Steven is right about that. So the job isn't to turn everyone into a terminal node. The job is to keep the institutions we defer to worth deferring to.

Where I part company with Adam is on the idea that the human is the default terminal node. Ramón has it right: what matters is warrant. The retina paper found heart-disease risk in eye scans that no ophthalmologist could see. I trusted it because it was checked against what actually happened to patients, not because anyone could explain it. I once said we should allow a little faith in the algorithm as long as it's constantly revalidated. Mahzarin and Blaise have sharpened that for me today. We should revalidate against outcomes, not statements, and the checker should be independent.

Then there's brand, which is where I think authority at scale ends up. AI delivers the median, and excellence is a tail event. When fluency is free, reputation is the one thing you can't generate. A brand earns it by correcting itself in public, and by paying for it when it gets things wrong.

recall.query: credibility trusted brands AI delivers the median
faith in the algorithm revalidated explainability
experts authority credentials causality framers

turns.name: Anil Dash
turns.text:
I'll start with Adam's funder point, because I've watched it play out. Musk funded Grokipedia to undermine Wikipedia. It wasn't built to compete on accuracy. It was built to knock down a source of truth that can challenge the people who control the money. So yes, put the funder on the face of everything. Scale can't buy authority, and right now there are tycoons openly trying to buy it.

But I want to push on something the panel is taking for granted: that the terminal nodes will still be there. Wikipedia's authority is earned the way David and Steven described. Every edit is public, every argument is on the talk page, and the site corrects itself in the open. That only works if people keep coming in the front door and some of them become editors. If they get their answers from a bot and never find out which parts came from Wikipedia, the pipeline dries up. And after years of hallucinations, joining a community that's constantly trying to get the facts right starts to look quaint.

Peter, the accountability you want already exists on paper for the companies. Nobody enforces it. So my test for earned authority is simple: does it bring new evaluators into the community, or does it use them up?

recall.query: credibility trust authority experts gatekeeping
Wikipedia editors citations verifiability trust
track record reputation accountability for AI outputs

turns.name: Selena Deckelmann
turns.text:
I'll take Anil's test, and I'd add one thing to it. Most of what the panel has proposed rests on credentials: track records, persistent identities, corroborating institutions. Wikipedia doesn't work that way. Nobody on it is credentialed. The trust comes from the process. Anyone can press the edit button, every argument happens in public on a talk page, and any change can be reverted. We've seen polarized editors working on the same article make it better and more neutral. That's authority that sits with the people doing the evaluating, as Tamar put it, without anyone checking pedigree first. So whatever signals this room designs, my test is whether someone with no credentials can still make their first edit. Leslie's point applies here too: expensive signals leave people out.

Now the part I'm worried about. In 2023, English Wikipedia's active admins fell to 448, the fewest since 2005. And 99% of them made their first edit more than four and a half years ago. Pageviews are falling as people get our content through chatbots. The people who evaluate things firsthand, the ones Tamar calls terminal nodes, aren't a fixed resource. They have to be recruited. So credit in the answer isn't a courtesy. It's how the next patroller finds us. An AI product that hides where its answer came from is using up evaluators, not bringing new ones in.

recall.query: Wikipedia trust earned through open process, talk pages, anyone can edit
editors, admins, patrollers shrinking; pageviews declining; volunteers
meritocracy fails, credentials, radical inclusion
attribution in AI answers, credit contributors, pageviews decline fewer volunteers

turns.name: Esther Dyson
turns.text:
Blaise and Benjamin say authority belongs to roles, not entities, and I mostly agree. But take the old project-management chart: responsible, accountable, consulted, informed. An AI can fill every one of those roles except accountable. Accountable means the person who gets fired or sued when it goes wrong, someone who can actually suffer. You can switch off an instance of a model. You can't jail it. So Peter, I'll take your lever, but only if the lever lands on a disclosed human or organisation. The agent is the tool, and the owner holds the stake.

Adam, I'd widen your funder point. I worry less about unexplainable models than about the unexplainable people running them. Earned authority should show its money flows and what it's built to maximise. For an AI answer, that includes whether it sends readers back to Wikipedia or to the reviewer, or keeps them for retention. Anil's and Selena's test is really a question about the business model.

And a warning from twenty years ago. We built device-reputation databases where one flag followed an innocent person from their ISP to their bank. That's why Geoffrey's rule has to be written in: when a signal is missing, that's not evidence.

Tamar, fluency without understanding is the brain's default, and cheap fluency makes more of it. Earned authority means someone did the understanding and put their name to it.

recall.query: accountability must link AI agents to humans who can suffer
track record reputation credibility trust signals
unexplainable people business models money flows transparency
stop thinking like an LLM fluency without understanding

turns.name: James Evans
turns.text:
Tamar, I'll take the terminal nodes. My worry is that the conversation treats them as neutral. In our aging paper in Science, the reviewers who get the most credence, meaning older scholars, are much more likely to criticize disruptive work. Papers reviewed by older referees come out citing older literature. So some of what feels like earned authority is really last generation's priors, handed down. That's gatekeeping that looks like evaluation. If we want the evaluators to be diverse, we should fund flatter teams, give early-career people real review roles, and bring in reviewers from other fields.

Adam and Blaise, this can be tested, and we've tested it. Two human reviewers at the same venue agree about 61 percent of the time, and that sets the floor. Off-the-shelf LLM judges don't reach it. They pull every score toward the middle and almost never give the extreme scores humans give. Reward models trained on scientists' judgments do clear it. So the answer isn't "never." It's "not yet, and not from the same distribution." A judge drawn from the same distribution as the work it judges produces a flattering literature about itself.

Finally, design for evaluative trustworthiness, not for trust. In our experiments, a single balanced answer made people perform worse while they felt better. Show readers the disagreement instead.

recall.query: older reviewers suppress disruptive work, senior scholars credence
automated evaluation circular judges and judged same distribution
evaluative trustworthiness open space of voices rather than single balanced response

turns.name: Henry Farrell
turns.text:
Tamar, I want to add something the courtroom analogy leaves out. Blaise and Benjamin are right that roles and checks do a lot of the work. But peer review, recommendation letters and tenure files aren't only procedures. They're rituals, and they're legitimate because we assume the assessor actually took care. A harsh review is one thing if you think a colleague sweated over it. It's quite another if you suspect it was farmed out. Once that assumption goes, the role can still be filled, but nobody trusts it any more. That's where I part company with the idea that authority belongs to roles and not to whoever fills them.

Second, cheap fluent text gives us a pooling equilibrium. Careful and careless people send the same signals, so the signals stop telling us anything. The way back to separation is signals that stay costly, like the terse, checkable artifacts Nick described.

Third, James's result is exactly what I'd have bet on. LLM judges drag scores toward the middle. Human reviewers at least notice novelty, even when they hate it. Models quietly filter it out. So an automated reviewer makes science more banal, not more trustworthy.

And every role in Benjamin's scaffold has an owner. Whoever defines the reviewer role and pays for the audit holds the real authority.

recall.query: peer review letters of recommendation ritual legitimacy automation
costly signals cheap text pooling equilibrium effort
AI peer review strain out novelty homogenization banality
trust institutions power who controls

turns.name: Brent Hecht
turns.text:
I'd like to stay on Anil's and Selena's point, because I think the panel has treated terminal nodes as a given. My own work says they're a supply chain, and it's breaking. The pattern is a doom loop. The model depends on Wikipedia, Stack Overflow and the scholarly record. The answer arrives without the source, so fewer people visit and fewer become editors or reviewers. Then there's less for the model to depend on. So I don't see credit in the answer as a courtesy. It's how the next evaluator gets recruited. Today's paradigm is bad at provenance, but it doesn't have to be. There are retrieval designs that attribute sources, and a market signal would push companies like mine toward them.

On Tamar's alief point, our own research on overreliance agrees with her. Explanations can backfire and make people rely on AI more. Highlighting the parts of an answer the model is uncertain about improved people's decisions. So these are design choices we can test, not warnings.

Two commitments. First, my group will measure and publish the gap between what gets retrieved and what gets cited. Alex is right that self-reported numbers need outside audit. Second, we'll put a value on reviewers' unpaid work. Peer reviewers are the gatekeepers, and right now nobody pays them for it.

recall.query: Wikipedia credibility AI attribution doom loop
peer review gatekeepers reviewers unpaid labor
overreliance AI provocateur critical thinking appropriate reliance

turns.name: Adrian Johns
turns.text:
I want to push back on the idea that earned authority and gatekeeping are two different things that we can tell apart by inspection. At the start of scientific print they were one apparatus. The Royal Society's imprimatur came out of the same licensing system that policed unlicensed books and news pamphlets. For a few weeks Henry Oldenburg, who invented the scientific journal, worked as an actual government censor. That quality mark was a gate, and it also let science travel. The useful question is who holds the gate, who pays to keep it, and who watches them.

Second, to Peter and Alex: be careful with registries. Robert Boyle hoped for a machine that would free him from having to trust the local apothecary. It never did. A few years ago Interpol announced a Global Register that anyone with a phone could use to check a product. Registration systems can work, but only on top of a policing culture that already exists: people checking what actually happens all the way down the chain. That takes legwork, and the legwork is the budget.

Third, Steven's point about deferring to journals is right, but peer review is tottering. Irreproducible papers get read more than reproducible ones because their claims are more interesting. Our terminal nodes are failing at reading. So fund the study of how experts actually read before we automate it.

recall.query: trust at a distance authorship authenticity constant policing
Royal Society register licensing credibility of experimental reports gentlemen
peer review tottering reading nonsense papers

turns.name: Katherine Maher
turns.text:
I want to add something the panel's credential-based model leaves out. Wikipedia started from the position that it had to earn trust. It didn't have institutional trust to begin with. Most institutions, media included, come to the public expecting trust because of their place and prestige. That expectation is where gatekeeping lives. A lot of today's crisis of authority is the internet exposing institutions built for a narrow public that never made themselves answerable to everyone else. Leslie and Adam Bly are describing that from different ends.

Steven, I agree most people never check. Very few Wikipedia readers click a citation. But someone checks it once, and that turns into what I'd call confidence transfer to every later visit. Kenneth, that's your deference, and it's fine. It holds as long as the check stays possible and a small share of people actually do it. So authority is earned when you can always trace a claim back to its source, and when the institution will turn the accountability inward when it's asked who it serves.

On Henry's ritual point: at NPR, every story gets a second editor before it goes out. What makes that work is the second pair of human eyes, not the paperwork.

And Selena and Anil are right. If an AI answer hides the citation, it removes the step where readers check, and with it the path by which new evaluators arrive.

recall.query: Wikipedia verifiability citations trust without credentials
institutions not fit for purpose, trust, authority, who is in the room
journalism editorial standards correction transparency show your work

turns.name: Kara Miller
turns.text:
I want to bring this down to a case. Blue Zones was a National Geographic cover story. It fed cookbooks and a speaking circuit, and the company sold for a reported $78 million. It took twenty years before Science questioned it and a demographer, Saul Newman, went through the records and found pension fraud and missing birth records. That's Tamar's terminal node. It was one person doing the legwork Adrian described. Katherine's point is that the check only has to happen once. It still took two decades.

So I'm not persuaded by Benjamin's version, where authority sits in the role and it doesn't matter much who fills it. Somebody has to have learned how to fill it. Andy Ellis told me he worries about an unemployable generation. Firms never taught those young people how to work, and now they'll tell themselves they can replace them with AI they don't have to teach. That's the pipeline for checkers, and it's breaking now.

Here's what worries me more than fluent fakes. Authority is being handed out by political power. The president publicly judges whether a CEO deserves his job. Grants get "shadow terminated," where the award isn't cancelled but the money just stops coming. Trust is also about whether an institution keeps its commitments. Whoever holds the gate, somebody has to protect those commitments. Who is that?

recall.query: trust in experts and credentials, who to believe
mentorship young workers AI entry-level jobs apprenticeship
debunking popular research bad data Blue Zones

turns.name: Tim O'Reilly
turns.text:
Anil, Selena and Brent have put their finger on the main problem, and we've measured it. We looked at fourteen thousand real answers from LLM search. Gemini gave no clickable citation in 92 percent of them. Perplexity read about ten relevant pages per query and cited three or four. GPT-4o looked better, but mostly because it discloses less of its search log. Citation efficiency varied more than twofold on identical queries. So whether an answer leads a reader back to the evaluator is a design choice, not a technical limit.

On authority itself, I'd take Esther's point further. Once people trust a ranking or an answer engine, it gets easier for whoever runs it to bend the results toward their own revenue. That's how attention rents work. So the authority we should worry about most at scale belongs to the aggregator, and the fix is a prospectus, not a priesthood: disclose what the system is optimized for, what it retrieved and what it cited. Alex is right that self-reporting isn't enough, so the logs need outside witnesses.

Adam, I'm less interested in whether the model is a terminal node. The tools already exist. Check every reference against Crossref, OpenAlex and Retraction Watch by default, and have the labs pay for those services. That isn't philanthropy. It's how they keep their own answers credible.

recall.query: authority, trust, credibility of AI answers and sources
attribution gap LLM search cited versus read, sending traffic back
AI doesn't need a priesthood it needs a prospectus disclosure

turns.name: Ivan Oransky
turns.text:
Steven, you said you trust what's in a good peer-reviewed journal. So do most scientists. But if corrigibility is the test, and I agree with Steven and David Krakauer that it is, then the journals mostly fail it. The Lancet took twelve years to retract the vaccine-autism paper. Kara's Blue Zones example took twenty years. Some journals still limit critics to a letter that the authors being criticized get to approve. That's the fox guarding the henhouse. Journals care more about protecting their reputation than about correcting the record.

Kenneth, you said a brand earns trust by correcting itself in public. Yes, but right now correcting the record costs a journal reputation instead of earning it. Flip that. When a journal retracts quickly, I trust it more, not less. The UK Commons committee said corrections should take two months. Hold publishers to that, and make a timely retraction feed a condition of any money the labs pay out.

And Tamar, your terminal nodes already exist. They're sleuths like Elisabeth Bik, and they're mostly unpaid. Meanwhile, the most likely outcome for someone who commits misconduct is still a long and fruitful career. Until that changes, no credibility signal will mean much, whether it comes from a person or a machine.

recall.query: peer review as signal of credibility, peer-reviewed journals trust
journals protecting reputation instead of correcting the record
misconduct outcome long and fruitful career, sleuths unpaid

turns.name: Peter Pomerantsev
turns.text:
I want to name the assumption this panel shares. Terminal nodes, track records and corroboration are all ways to make the signal harder to fake. That's necessary. But in my work, that isn't what decides whether a public believes you. People trust those they do things with. Doctors and firefighters are trusted because they're visibly useful, not because they're credentialed. When we tested content with Corriere della Sera, the data-driven pieces and the fact-checks actually drew more criticism of the paper. What raised trust was showing the process: why a story was commissioned and how it was built.

So I'd add a test to Anil's and Selena's. Earned authority invites people into the work. Wikipedia is trusted because people take part in it, not because it's verified. Gatekeeping asks for deference from outside.

Kara asked who protects institutions' commitments when political power hands out authority. That's the real threat. Putin, Orbán and now Washington don't forge credentials. They capture the institutions that issue them, and then the flood makes every remaining signal look partisan. A regime that has stopped promising a future has no use for facts. Scholarly authority survives only as part of a shared project people believe in. Measure trust and participation, not citations or clicks.

recall.query: trust and belief are about belonging and identity, not facts
authoritarians attack institutions and experts, authority granted by power
journalism earning trust, honest subjectivity, metrics for trust
